notes: Centre Party (Kekkonen's party) moved from MD slot 14 to ruling slot 1 as instructed. Coalition slot 2 keeps the National Coalition Party (MD placement), although it is in opposition; Koivisto's real partners are SDP (3), Swedish People's Party (14, moved from MD 15 to the regional slot with popularity), TPSL (18) and SKDL (19, as the 'Finnish road' popular front; the SKP itself sits in 4). Taistoite minority in 6, Soviet-embassy clientele in 7, Kekkonen's Tamminiemi court in 13. Slots 8, 9, 11, 12 are small foreign-student circles; slot 10 is the real Tatar congregation.

0.name: Suojelupoliisi
0.text:
The Finnish Security Police was created in 1949 to replace the State Police, which the communists had controlled during the post-war 'years of danger'. Under the Ministry of the Interior it watches the Communist Party, Soviet intelligence officers and foreign agents, quietly trading information with Swedish and other Western services while publicly respecting the strict neutrality demanded by President Kekkonen.

Its officers are anti-communist by background and conviction, many of them shaped by the war years. They regard the Soviet embassy and the communist-led unions as the real threat to Finnish independence and distrust politicians who court Moscow. Should the democratic order collapse into crisis, Supo's files, informants and links to the officer corps would make it the core of a Western-leaning emergency regime.

1.name: Keskustapuolue
1.text:
The Centre Party is the old Agrarian League, renamed in 1965 to reach voters beyond the shrinking countryside. It is the party of President Urho Kekkonen, in office since 1956 and re-elected in 1968, and under its chairman Johannes Virolainen it sits in Mauno Koivisto's broad cabinet alongside the Social Democrats and the People's Democrats. Parliamentary elections are due in March 1970.

The party stands for family farms, regional policy, rural credit and the Paasikivi–Kekkonen line of neutrality and trust with Moscow, which it presents as the guarantee of Finnish independence. Its base is the smallholders and villages of the north and east. Its leverage is the presidency itself, the farmers' cooperatives and the Soviet goodwill that makes it indispensable in every coalition.

2.name: Kansallinen Kokoomus
2.text:
The National Coalition Party is Finland's main bourgeois party, founded in 1918 by monarchist and conservative Finns. Led since 1965 by Juha Rihtniemi, it has been in opposition since the left's victory of 1966 and is kept out of government by Moscow's open distrust and by President Kekkonen, who doubts its loyalty to his eastern policy. It expects strong gains in the March 1970 elections.

The party defends private enterprise, lower taxes, the Lutheran church, national defence and closer economic ties with Western Europe and the Nordic states. Its younger generation is moving towards a moderate, reformist conservatism that accepts the official line on the Soviet Union. Its base is the urban middle class, business, officials and landowners, and its leverage lies in banks, industry and the press.

3.name: Suomen Sosialidemokraattinen Puolue
3.text:
The Social Democratic Party of Finland has been the largest party in parliament since its victory in 1966. Chairman Rafael Paasio then formed the first cabinet since 1948 to include the communist-led left, and since March 1968 the Bank of Finland governor Mauno Koivisto heads a broad coalition of Social Democrats, Centre, People's Democrats, the Swedish People's Party and the Skogist left. The party has made its peace with President Kekkonen.

The SDP stands for a Nordic welfare state, comprehensive schooling, pensions and centralised incomes agreements, and it leads the reunited trade union confederation SAK. It accepts neutrality and Soviet trade while looking to Sweden and Western Europe for its model. Its base is the industrial working class and public employees, its leverage the unions and the premiership.

4.name: Suomen Kommunistinen Puolue
4.text:
The Communist Party of Finland, founded in Moscow in 1918 and legal since 1944, is the core of the People's Democratic League. Chairman Aarne Saarinen, a former trade union leader, heads a reform-minded majority that criticised the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968. The April 1969 congress ended with the hardline minority walking out, and Moscow is pressing hard for reunification.

The party is Marxist-Leninist and a loyal member of the world communist movement, but its majority seeks a parliamentary road and partnership with the Social Democrats in government. It is strong among industrial, construction and forest workers, in the unions and in the poor north and east. Its leverage lies in disciplined cadres, its ministers in the cabinet and its standing in Moscow.

5.name: Sadankomitea
5.text:
The Committee of 100 was founded in Helsinki in 1963 on the model of Bertrand Russell's British committee and has become the spearhead of Finland's New Left. Its young intellectuals, students and artists campaign against nuclear weapons, conscription, the Vietnam War and the military culture of the 1918 victors, and they share the mood of the radicals who occupied the Old Student House in November 1968.

The committee demands the right to refuse military service, disarmament, solidarity with liberation movements and a radical democratisation of universities and culture. It distrusts both superpowers but is drifting steadily towards Marxism. Its base is the Helsinki student milieu, the cultural press and radio, and its leverage lies in civil disobedience, publicity and its influence on a restless generation.

6.name: Taistolaiset
6.text:
The Taistoites are the hardline minority of the Communist Party of Finland, grouped around the veteran functionary Taisto Sinisalo. They defended the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia, walked out of the April 1969 party congress and now run their own district organisations, newspapers and youth groups, enjoying the open favour of the Soviet embassy and the CPSU.

They reject the majority's parliamentary road as revisionism and preach class struggle, proletarian internationalism and unconditional loyalty to the Soviet Union. Their strongholds are old industrial districts in the south and, increasingly, radicalised students, writers and theatre people. Their leverage lies in Moscow's backing, which no Finnish government can ignore, and in a fervent, disciplined following ready to take over the party.

7.name: Tehtaankadun piiri
7.text:
Tehtaankatu, the Helsinki street of the Soviet embassy, has become shorthand for Moscow's hand in Finnish politics. Around the embassy and its KGB residency stands a circle of politicians, officials, editors and businessmen from every party who cultivate a personal Soviet contact, a 'house Russian', and seek favours, trade deals and promotion through him. Since the night frost of 1958 and the note crisis of 1961, ambitious Finns know that careers are made and ended on Tehtaankatu.

The circle believes not in communism but in power. It would turn Finlandisation into a system: a managed press, a pliant parliament, purged anti-Soviet officers and a state that consults the embassy before deciding. Its leverage is Soviet favour, eastern trade licences and the fear of displeasing the great neighbour.

8.name: Ershad-piiri
8.text:
The Ershad Circle is a handful of Iranian students and young engineers in Helsinki and Otaniemi who meet for Friday prayers and discussion in private flats. They take their name and ideas from the Hosseiniyeh Ershad in Tehran, where the sociologist Ali Shariati lectures to packed halls on Islam as a doctrine of justice and liberation, and they read Mehdi Bazargan, founder of the suppressed Freedom Movement of Iran.

The circle preaches a modern, socially conscious Shiism that rejects both clerical conservatism and Marxist atheism. It opposes the Shah's autocracy and American influence in Iran but admires Nordic democracy and welfare. It has no funds or institutions; its leverage lies in contacts with Iranian Muslim student associations in Western Europe and in the educated cadres it hopes to send home.

9.name: Najafin lähetit
9.text:
The Messengers of Najaf are a few devout Iranian and Iraqi students in Finland who pass on the letters, rulings and pamphlets of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled by the Shah in 1964 and living in the Iraqi shrine city of Najaf since 1965. The material reaches them through religious Iranian student groups in West Germany and Britain.

The circle holds that the Shah's regime is illegitimate and that Shia jurists must guide Muslims in political as well as religious matters. It condemns Israel, American power and the land and women's reforms of the Shah's White Revolution, and keeps apart from secular leftist Iranians. It has no public presence; its leverage rests on the zeal of its members and their ties to the clerical opposition abroad.

10.name: Suomen Islam-seurakunta
10.text:
The Finnish Islamic Congregation is the religious body of the Finnish Tatars, a community of under a thousand Muslims descended from merchants who came from the Volga region in the late nineteenth century. Registered in 1925 under the new law on freedom of religion, it is among the oldest officially recognised Muslim congregations in Western Europe and keeps its prayer hall and school in the Tatar house on Fredrikinkatu in Helsinki.

The congregation follows Hanafi Sunni Islam and is resolutely loyal, apolitical and patriotic; Tatar men fought for Finland in the Winter and Continuation Wars. It cultivates its Turkic language, Islamic education and ties with Turkey, and keeps clear of radical movements. Its leverage is modest, resting on respected merchant families and its reputation as a model minority.

11.name: Kalifaatin kutsu
11.text:
The Call of the Caliphate is a tiny study group of Arab students, mostly Palestinians and Jordanians, at the technical and medical faculties in Helsinki. They receive the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Sheikh Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, through its cells among Arab students in West Germany and Austria.

The group teaches that the Muslim world must be reunited under a restored caliphate, that nationalist regimes, monarchies and parliaments are illegitimate, and that Israel has no right to exist. It rejects both American capitalism and Soviet communism as systems of unbelief. It counts no more than a few sympathisers; its leverage lies in persistent proselytising and links to the party's clandestine organisation in the Arab world.

12.name: Muslimiopiskelijoiden piiri
12.text:
The Muslim Students' Circle brings together Egyptian, Sudanese and Pakistani students with a few young Finnish Tatars in Helsinki for Quran study, lectures and charitable work. It looks for guidance to the Muslim Brotherhood exiles abroad, above all Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre in Geneva, and to the Muslim World League founded in Mecca in 1962, whose literature it distributes.

The circle reads Hassan al-Banna, Abul A'la Maududi and Sayyid Qutb, hanged in Cairo in 1966, and calls for an Islamic order built through education, preaching and lawful activity. It opposes Nasser's secular socialism, communism and Western materialism alike, and hopes to give Finland a proper mosque. Its leverage is small, resting on student networks and the patronage of Saudi-funded Islamic institutions.

13.name: Tamminiemen hovi
13.text:
Tamminiemi, the seaside villa of President Urho Kekkonen, is the real seat of power in Finland. Around it stands a court of trusted advisers, officials, diplomats, editors and businessmen whose standing depends on the president's favour, led by his former secretary and presumed heir, Foreign Minister Ahti Karjalainen. Fourteen years into his rule, Kekkonen decides who governs, which parties are acceptable to Moscow and when parliament is dissolved.

The court treats parties as instruments and neutrality as a reason of state above debate. It favours a strong presidency, consensus through incomes agreements, careful restraint towards the Soviet Union and expanding trade with both East and West. Its leverage lies in the presidency's sweeping constitutional powers, Kekkonen's personal channel to the Kremlin and the careers it can make or break.

14.name: Svenska folkpartiet i Finland
14.text:
The Swedish People's Party is the political home of Finland's Swedish-speaking minority, under seven per cent of the population and concentrated on the southern and western coasts. Founded in 1906 and led since 1966 by the political scientist Jan-Magnus Jansson, it belongs to Mauno Koivisto's broad coalition and supplies ministers alongside the Social Democrats and the Centre.

The party defends Swedish-language schools, universities, courts and bilingual municipalities, together with a liberal, Nordic-minded market economy and close cooperation with Sweden. It unites the fishermen and farmers of Ostrobothnia and the archipelago with Helsinki's old merchant and banking families. Its leverage lies in its role as a dependable coalition partner, its wealthy patrons and its weight in finance and industry.

15.name: Suomen Työnantajain Keskusliitto
15.text:
The Finnish Employers' Confederation, founded in 1907, speaks for the forest, metal and textile industries that earn Finland's living. Together with the two great commercial banks, Kansallis-Osake-Pankki and the Union Bank of Finland, around which rival industrial groups cluster, it forms the inner circle of Finnish capital. In 1968 it signed the first comprehensive incomes policy agreement with the unions under the national conciliator Keijo Liinamaa.

The employers want wage restraint, export competitiveness after the 1967 devaluation, free trade through Finland's EFTA association and eventually an arrangement with the Common Market, while also profiting from the clearing trade with the Soviet Union. Their leverage lies in control of investment, credit and exports, and in the ear of every government, including one with communist ministers.

16.name: Liberaalinen Kansanpuolue
16.text:
The Liberal People's Party was formed in 1965 by the merger of the Finnish People's Party and the Liberal League, heirs of the National Progressive Party that wrote the republican constitution of 1919. Led since 1968 by the historian Mikko Juva, it is a small opposition party with about six per cent of the vote, strongest among the educated urban middle class.

The party stands for individual liberty, a market economy with social responsibility, educational reform, freedom of expression and Western European integration within the bounds of neutrality. It champions entrepreneurs, teachers, civil servants and the professions against both socialist planning and agrarian subsidies. Its leverage lies in its intellectual prestige and its value as a swing partner for bourgeois or centre-left cabinets.

17.name: Suomen Luonnonsuojeluliitto
17.text:
The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, founded in 1938, unites local and regional societies of naturalists, scientists, teachers and hikers. With 1970 proclaimed European Conservation Year by the Council of Europe, it is shedding its old image as a guardian of rare plants and birds and turning to the new threats of river regulation, mining, clear-cutting and the industrial pollution of lakes and the Baltic.

The association calls for new national parks in Lapland, protection of the remaining rapids and wilderness, controls on effluent from pulp mills and a national environmental administration. Its supporters range from conservative landowners to young radicals who see pollution as the price of unrestrained growth. Its leverage lies in scientific authority, public sympathy and growing press interest in the environment.

18.name: Työväen ja Pienviljelijäin Sosialidemokraattinen Liitto
18.english: Social Democratic Union of Workers and Smallholders
18.text:
The Social Democratic Union of Workers and Smallholders was formed in 1959 by the followers of Emil Skog, who broke with Väinö Tanner's Social Democratic leadership over its hostility to President Kekkonen and the Soviet Union. The Skogists held key posts in the trade union confederation SAK during the labour split of the 1960s and now sit in Mauno Koivisto's coalition, though their electorate is dwindling.

The union combines social democracy with unconditional support for the Paasikivi–Kekkonen line and friendship with the Soviet Union. It speaks for workers and small farmers in the forest and rural districts of central and eastern Finland. Its leverage lies in Kekkonen's patronage and its usefulness as a bridge between the Social Democrats, the Centre and the communists.
18.wiki: Social Democratic Union of Workers and Smallholders

19.name: Suomen Kansan Demokraattinen Liitto
19.text:
The Finnish People's Democratic League was founded in 1944 as the legal front of communists and left socialists and has won around a fifth of the vote ever since. Led since 1967 by Ele Alenius, a non-communist socialist, it returned to government in 1966 after eighteen years in opposition and holds ministries in Mauno Koivisto's cabinet.

Alenius argues for a 'Finnish road to socialism': a parliamentary, pluralist transformation through nationalisation, planning and alliance with the Social Democrats, independent of foreign models. The League supports neutrality and friendship with the Soviet Union but regretted the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia. Its base is industrial workers, small farmers of the north and east and the left intelligentsia; its leverage is its mass vote.

20.name: Suomen Maaseudun Puolue
20.text:
The Finnish Rural Party was founded in 1959 as the Smallholders' Party by Veikko Vennamo, a former Agrarian League official who fell out with Urho Kekkonen and the party leadership, and took its present name in 1966. It holds a single seat in parliament, but Vennamo's furious speeches are drawing huge crowds of 'forgotten people' in the countryside ahead of the March 1970 elections.

The party speaks for the small farmers and rural workers ruined by the mechanisation of agriculture, the field reservation scheme and the great migration to the cities and Sweden. It attacks the 'gentlemen' of Helsinki, the bureaucracy, corruption and the Centre Party establishment, and accuses Kekkonen of autocracy. Its leverage lies in rural anger and Vennamo's demagogic talent.

21.name: Sinimustat
21.text:
The Blue-Blacks take their name from the uniformed youth league of the Patriotic People's Movement (IKL), Finland's fascist party of the 1930s, which was dissolved in 1944 under the armistice with the Soviet Union. A scattering of ageing IKL veterans, former members of the Academic Karelia Society and a few young admirers keep its ideas alive in private study circles, memorial evenings and duplicated leaflets.

They dream of a Greater Finland, an authoritarian corporate state and a reckoning with communists, Finlandisation and submissive politicians. They despise the Soviet Union, liberal democracy and the left-wing student radicals. Their influence is negligible and the Security Police watches them closely, but in a national crisis they could draw on veterans' bitterness and deep-rooted anti-Russian feeling.

22.name: Puolustusvoimat
22.text:
The Finnish Defence Forces have been commanded since 1969 by General Yrjö Keinonen, under the president as commander-in-chief. Limited by the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty to a small peacetime force and barred from bombers and submarines, they rely on universal conscription to raise a large wartime army of reservists. The officer corps was forged in the Winter and Continuation Wars.

The officers profess strict loyalty to the president and the policy of neutrality, but privately see the Soviet Union as the only realistic threat and doubt the left's commitment to defence. They seek modern equipment from both East and West and a territorial defence of the entire country. Their leverage lies in their wartime prestige, the vast reserve and the veterans' associations.

23.name: Haus Hessen
23.text:
In October 1918 the Finnish parliament elected Prince Frederick Charles of Hesse King of Finland, only for him to renounce the throne two months later after Germany's defeat. His surviving sons are Landgrave Philipp, head of the House of Hesse, and Prince Wolfgang, once designated Crown Prince of Finland; both live in West Germany and have never pressed the claim.

Finnish monarchism survives only as a memory among elderly conservatives, some old families and veterans of the White Army of 1918, who see a crown as a symbol above party strife and a link to Western Europe. A Hessian monarchy would stand for constitutional order, the Lutheran church and national unity. Its leverage is purely symbolic and depends on a national crisis that discredits the republic.
